title: UI/UX Design: Understanding the Experience
idea: One product, two screens: a phone and a browser. Gather will follow you through every unit.
notes:
Welcome to SVCB3003 UI & UX Design. Over 45 instructional hours and five units, you will learn how designers understand people, structure ideas, and turn them into interfaces that work on phones and on the web.

Point to the cover: the phone and the browser window are the same product, a university event registration platform we will call Gather. We will return to Gather in almost every unit, so you can watch one idea travel from research, to personas, to flows, to wireframes, to a tested prototype.

Course references: Yablonski, Laws of UX; Garrett, The Elements of User Experience; Marsh, UX for Beginners; Kraft, User Experience Innovation; Tullis and Albert, Measuring the User Experience.

Ask: "What app did you use today without thinking about it? Why was it easy?"

title: By the end, you will build real experiences.
idea: Six outcomes, from explaining UX and UI to building working mobile and web prototypes.
notes:
This course moves from understanding to making. Read the six outcomes aloud and connect each one to a unit: outcomes one and two come from Unit 1, three from Unit 2, four from Unit 3, five from Unit 4, and the sixth, the capstone, is built in Units 4 and 5.

Stress that the final outcome is practical: you will create mobile and web wireframes and working prototypes. Everything before that exists to make those wireframes smarter, more inclusive, and testable.

The outcomes here are written to match the course description; instructors should align the wording with the official course outline if it differs.

Teaching tip: ask students to rate their confidence in each outcome from one to five now, and again at the end of the course.

title: Good design is invisible. Bad design is a mystery.
idea: When design works you do not notice it. When it fails, people blame themselves.
notes:
Start with the everyday, because design is not only screens. Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things (supplementary reading, not on the course list) gave us a vocabulary: affordances are what an object lets you do; signifiers tell you where to act; mapping is how controls relate to results; feedback tells you what just happened.

Walk through the four vignettes. The door whose handle says pull but whose sign says push has conflicting signals. The stove with four knobs and four burners forces you to guess the mapping. A toggle without a clear state label leaves you unsure whether it shows what is on, or what will happen if you tap. An error that says only "Invalid input" gives no help.

Each one is a UX problem in the physical or digital world. Close with the reflection prompt and let students share two or three examples.

title: Five units. One continuous process.
idea: Five units move from understanding, to strategy, research, craft and testing.
notes:
Use this slide as the map for the whole course. Each unit is a step up: Unit 1 builds the vocabulary and mindset; Unit 2 turns that mindset into a strategy, using design thinking, sprints and competitive analysis; Unit 3 gives you research and empathy tools to understand users; Unit 4 teaches the visual and structural decisions that shape the interface, ending in wireframes; and Unit 5 makes those wireframes interactive, tests them, and improves them.

Notice the Gather milestone under each step. Your assignments follow the same rhythm, so by Unit 5 you will have documented an evidence-based design.

The process is not a straight line. Real teams loop back after testing, which is why "iterate" sits above the staircase. Ask students: "Which step do you expect to be hardest?"

title: Same product. Two different questions.
idea: UX asks how it works for a person. UI asks how it looks and responds.
notes:
Here is the same registration screen seen through two lenses. User Experience, UX, covers the whole journey: how easy it is to find the event, how many steps registration takes, whether you trust what happens with your data, and how you recover from a mistake. User Interface, UI, is the layer you see and touch: colour, type, spacing, buttons, fields, and how they respond.

A helpful analogy is a restaurant. UI is the menu design, plates and lighting. UX is whether you are seated quickly, understand the menu, receive your order correctly, and leave wanting to return.

Key message: UI is part of UX, not a synonym for it. A beautiful interface can still deliver a poor experience, and a plain interface can work wonderfully. Marsh's UX for Beginners offers a gentle introduction to this distinction.

Activity: ask students to name one UX decision and one UI decision visible on this screen.

title: Design decides whether people succeed.
idea: Design decides whether people finish the task or give up.
notes:
Why does this field exist? Because interfaces sit between people and the things they need to do: travel somewhere, talk to a friend, pay a bill, join an event. When the interface is clear, people succeed and barely notice it. When it is confusing, they lose time, make mistakes, or give up.

Purpose: UI/UX design helps people reach their goals with less effort and more confidence. Significance: it shapes trust, cost, safety and inclusion. Influence: it affects real users every day, in small moments.

The three schematic screens on the right show moments where UX is felt. A map must be readable at a glance while moving. A chat app reassures you through message status. A payment screen must make the total and the way back obvious. These are simplified original drawings, not official screenshots.

Ask: "Which of these moments would hurt most if it were badly designed?"

title: Five qualities of a good experience.
idea: Usability, usefulness, accessibility, clarity and satisfaction: five questions to ask of any product.
notes:
Introduce the five qualities as the questions a good experience must answer. Usability: can people complete tasks effectively and efficiently? The international standard ISO 9241-11 defines usability as effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users and goals in a specified context. Usefulness: does it solve a real need, or is it a clever feature nobody wants? Accessibility: can people with different abilities and situations use it? Clarity: is it obvious what each element is and what to do next? Satisfaction: does the experience feel good, building confidence?

These overlap. A product can be usable but not useful, or delightful but inaccessible. Great experiences satisfy all five at once.

Link each quality to Gather on the right. Ask students to give a score out of five on each quality for an app they use daily, and say which is weakest.

title: Five planes. Abstract to concrete.
idea: Garrett's planes: Strategy, Scope, Structure, Skeleton, Surface. Decide the abstract first.
notes:
Jesse James Garrett's The Elements of User Experience describes five planes, built from the bottom up. Each plane depends on the ones beneath it, and decisions at lower planes constrain what is possible above.

Strategy: user needs and product objectives, the "why". Scope: functional specifications and content requirements, the "what". Structure: interaction design and information architecture, how pieces fit together and behave. Skeleton: interface design, navigation design and information design, the layout of controls and content. Surface: visual design, what the product looks and feels like.

Notice how beginners often jump straight to Surface, picking colours before knowing the strategy. The framework warns against that. If strategy is unclear, a beautiful surface cannot rescue it.

In Gather: strategy is helping students find events and helping the university grow participation. The surface we see on the cover is the last thing we decide.

title: Psychology you can design with.
idea: Jakob, Fitts, Hick, Miller, Doherty and Peak-End: psychology you can apply on a screen.
notes:
Jon Yablonski's Laws of UX collects principles from psychology that explain how people perceive, decide and remember. They are best treated as useful heuristics, not strict laws of nature.

Jakob's Law: users spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the same way. Fitts's Law: the time to reach a target depends on its distance and size, so make important targets large and close. Hick's Law: the time to decide increases with the number and complexity of choices. Miller's Law: working memory is limited, often quoted as around seven items plus or minus two, so chunk information. The Doherty Threshold: productivity soars when a system and its user interact at a pace of under roughly 400 ms. The Peak-End Rule: people judge an experience largely by its most intense point and its end.

Challenge students to find one example of each law in their phone's home screen.

title: UX takes part in every stage.
idea: Discover, define, design, develop, test, launch and learn: UX has a job at every stage.
notes:
Many people imagine UX as a design step in the middle. In reality UX contributes at every stage of the product development life cycle.

Discover: teams explore the opportunity; UX runs interviews, observation and competitor reviews. Define: teams agree scope and requirements; UX writes personas, problem statements and user stories. Design: UX creates flows, wireframes, prototypes and the visual interface. Develop: engineers build; UX supplies specs and checks the build matches, including accessibility. Test: quality assurance and usability testing find problems; UX triages them. Launch and learn: the team releases, monitors analytics and feedback, and feeds learning into the next cycle.

The cycle varies between companies; some use agile sprints instead of long phases. The point is that UX involvement early is cheaper than fixing problems late.

Bottom row shows what Gather would produce at each stage.

title: Be deep in one thing. Curious about many.
idea: A T-shaped designer goes deep in one skill and stays curious about the rest.
notes:
UX design is a team sport, and designers shape their careers along a spectrum. Specialists have deep expertise in one craft, such as UX research, interaction design, content design or accessibility. Generalists have broad skills across research, design and prototyping; they thrive in small teams and start-ups. T-shaped designers combine both: the vertical bar is depth in one area, the horizontal bar is the ability to understand and collaborate across disciplines. The T-shape metaphor was popularised by the design firm IDEO.

Career applications: UX appears in mobile apps, websites, games, healthcare, finance, education, government services, e-commerce and emerging areas such as AR and VR. Titles vary by company, so focus on the skills, not just the label.

Reflection: which letter do you want to become, and what is your first deep skill?

title: Every point of friction has a cost.
idea: Every confusing step loses some people. An illustrative funnel shows where.
notes:
Good UX is not only about delight; it is about outcomes. When an experience is clear, people engage more, complete more tasks, trust the product and recommend it.

The funnel shows a typical registration journey for Gather. At each step some people drop away. Friction, such as hard-to-find events, unclear details, a long form or no reminder, widens the leak. Removing friction narrows it. The shape here is illustrative only; we are not presenting real data, because every product is different.

The four cards connect design quality to business outcomes and show how you can measure each one: engagement (return visits, feature use), conversion (task completion, drop-off), trust (drop-off at sensitive steps, feedback) and satisfaction (System Usability Scale, Net Promoter Score, support tickets). Tullis and Albert's Measuring the User Experience details these metrics.

Key point: always measure before claiming a UX improvement worked.

title: Audit an app you already use.
idea: Audit an existing app: features, users, intentions, strengths and weaknesses, with evidence.
notes:
Unit 1 assignment: choose an existing application and audit it. Students identify its features, intended users and design intentions, then evaluate strengths and weaknesses.

Coach students to separate observation from opinion. "The search bar is at the top" is an observation. "The search is hard to reach with one hand" is an interpretation that needs evidence, perhaps a reference to Fitts's Law or a quick test with a classmate.

Encourage annotated screenshots and clear evidence for each judgement. Remind them to choose a product they can analyse in depth rather than a very complex one. The hypothetical audit card on this slide shows the level of detail expected; the format and length of submission are set by the instructor.

Success criteria: balanced analysis (both strengths and weaknesses), evidence from the interface, and links to concepts from this unit such as the five planes and the laws of UX.

title: Three ways to open the door.
idea: Universal, inclusive and equity-focused design: three ways to open the door.
notes:
Universal, inclusive and equity-focused design are related but different, and students often mix them up.

Universal design aims for one design usable by as many people as possible without special adaptation. The Center for Universal Design at North Carolina State University published seven principles in 1997, such as equitable use, flexibility in use, and simple and intuitive use.

Inclusive design is a practice and a process. Microsoft's Inclusive Design toolkit frames three ideas: recognise exclusion, solve for one and extend to many, and learn from human diversity. The aim is multiple ways in, such as registering by app, QR code or at a desk.

Equity-focused design recognises that people start from different places. Equal access is not always fair, so we give more support where barriers are greater, for example a low-data mode for students with weak connections.

Ask: "Which of these would you choose first for Gather, and why?"

title: Great products balance two sets of needs.
idea: Users need to succeed and the business needs to sustain. Good products serve both.
notes:
User-centred design starts from people: their goals, tasks, contexts and limitations. Business-centred thinking starts from the organisation: revenue, brand, risk, cost and strategy. Neither is wrong. Problems appear when one side dominates. A product that serves only business goals feels manipulative; one that ignores business realities may never be built or sustained.

The overlap is the sweet spot, where meeting user needs also creates organisational value. Christian Kraft's User Experience Innovation discusses how UX and business strategy can reinforce each other.

The sliders show three real trade-offs in Gather. Collecting more data helps reporting but slows sign-up. Sponsor visibility helps funding but can clutter the interface. More reminders may raise attendance but can annoy. Good designers do not pretend trade-offs do not exist; they make a decision, record the reasoning, and test it.

Discussion: whose needs does your favourite app serve first?

title: Anyone can be disabled by a design.
idea: Disability can be permanent, temporary or situational. Design can disable anyone.
notes:
Accessibility means designing so people with different abilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with a product. The key idea on this slide, from Microsoft's Inclusive Design toolkit, is that disability is not only permanent. It is a mismatch between a person and their environment.

Read across a row. Someone with one arm has a permanent touch limitation; someone with an arm injury has a temporary one; a person holding a baby has a situational one. The same solution, such as one-handed use, helps all three. This is why accessible design benefits everyone.

The bottom strip shows the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. We apply them in the next slide.

Ask: "When was the last time you were temporarily or situationally limited when using your phone?"

title: Five accessibility checks you can run today.
idea: Five checks: readable text, contrast, keyboard, labels and touch targets.
notes:
Turn principles into habits with five practical checks.

Readable text: use body text of at least 16 px, generous line spacing, and short lines. Colour contrast: WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and user-interface components. The ratios in the contrast card are calculated from this deck's own palette. Notice that white text on our electric blue reaches only 4.36:1, so we use it only for large, bold labels and use a deeper blue for small text.

Keyboard navigation: everything should work with Tab, Enter and arrow keys, with a visible focus ring. Labels: never rely on a placeholder alone; it disappears. Interactions: make touch targets comfortably large (Apple suggests 44 points, Material Design 48 dp) and never communicate error by colour alone.

Activity: test one screen of your own work against all five checks.

title: Five modes. You will loop through them.
idea: Empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test. Expect to loop back.
notes:
Design thinking is a human-centred approach to solving problems. The version taught by the Stanford d.school has five modes: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test. IDEO and the Interaction Design Foundation describe similar sequences.

Empathise: understand people by observing and interviewing them. Define: synthesise what you learned into a clear problem statement. Ideate: generate many possible solutions before choosing. Prototype: make quick, inexpensive versions to think with. Test: put prototypes in front of users and learn.

The key message is that the process is iterative, not linear. Testing often reveals that you misunderstood the problem and sends you back to empathise. The return arrow on the slide represents that loop, and you can jump to any stage when needed.

The Gather row shows one small example per stage. Ask students to propose a different example for each stage.

title: Widen the field. Then narrow it.
idea: Diverge to generate many options, then converge to choose with reasons.
notes:
Great design alternates between two modes of thinking. Divergent thinking opens up possibilities: you generate many ideas, defer judgement and value quantity. Convergent thinking narrows: you compare ideas against criteria, combine the best, and decide.

The British Design Council's Double Diamond (2004) shows this twice. The first diamond is about the problem: Discover widens what you know through research, then Define narrows to a clear problem. The second diamond is about the solution: Develop widens by exploring ideas and prototypes, then Deliver narrows to a tested solution.

A common mistake is converging too early, picking the first good idea. Another is never converging, endlessly brainstorming. Good facilitators name the mode out loud: "For the next ten minutes we are diverging, no criticism."

In Gather, the team might sketch 20 registration ideas, then shortlist three using an impact versus effort comparison.

title: Months of debate, compressed into one week.
idea: Map, sketch, decide, prototype, test: five days from question to evidence.
notes:
The design sprint was developed by Jake Knapp at Google Ventures and described in the book Sprint (Knapp, Zeratsky and Kowitz, 2016). It is a structured five-day process for answering critical questions through design and testing with real customers.

Monday, Map: agree a long-term goal, map the challenge and choose a target. Tuesday, Sketch: gather inspiration and sketch solutions individually. Wednesday, Decide: review the sketches, vote and storyboard the winning idea. Thursday, Prototype: build a realistic prototype, a facade just good enough to test. Friday, Test: interview about five users while the team watches and notes patterns.

Benefits: fast decisions, learning before heavy investment, a shared understanding in the team and early evidence from users. Limitations: it needs commitment of the whole team and works best for focused questions.

For Gather, imagine a sprint goal: any student can register for an event without help.

title: Compare the options. Find the gaps.
idea: Compare the same tasks across products to find gaps and chances.
notes:
Competitive analysis means studying similar products to understand what they do well, where they cause problems and where opportunities remain. Competitors are not only direct rivals. For event registration, indirect alternatives include a group chat announcement or a campus web page.

The method: choose a set of competitors, define criteria from real user tasks, test the same tasks on each product, record evidence such as screenshots and task times, then look for gaps. Gaps become opportunities.

The grid on the slide is an illustrative example to show the technique. The ratings are hypotheses, not research findings, and the Gather column shows a design target, not a measured result. In your own assignment, you must base ratings on evidence from your own testing.

Warn against copying competitors blindly. The goal is to understand patterns, avoid known problems, and find where you can offer something better for your users.

title: Find what is broken. Fix it creatively.
idea: Assignment 2: find disadvantages, analyse competitors, propose solutions.
notes:
Unit 2 assignment: identify disadvantages in an existing product, perform a competitor analysis, and propose creative, user-focused solutions.

Remind students that the strongest submissions start from evidence, not opinions. Each disadvantage should be backed by a screenshot, a task attempt or a user comment. The competitor analysis should compare the same tasks across products, with clear criteria. The proposed solutions must link back to the problems found; avoid adding features simply because they are fashionable.

Encourage students to apply ideas from the unit: design thinking, divergent and convergent thinking, inclusive design, and the balance between user and business needs. A short sketch of each proposed solution helps the instructor see the thinking.

The mini grid on this slide is a hypothetical illustration of format. The exact submission format is set by the instructor.

title: Storyboards tell it. Mood boards feel it.
idea: A storyboard shows the sequence. A mood board sets tone and feeling.
notes:
Before drawing screens, designers often create two kinds of visual stories.

A storyboard is a sequence of panels showing a person moving through a scenario: the context, what they do, and how they feel. It originated in film and animation and is widely used in UX to align a team on the user's story. Keep drawings simple; stick figures are fine. Each panel should answer: where are they, what do they want, what happens next?

A mood board is a collage that explores the look, feel and tone of a product: colours, typography, imagery, textures and keywords. It helps teams agree on a direction before investing in detailed UI, and it makes visual decisions intentional rather than arbitrary.

In Gather, the storyboard follows Aisha from seeing a poster to scanning a QR ticket. The mood board explores a feeling that is energetic, friendly and trustworthy.

Activity: have students sketch a four-panel storyboard in five minutes.

title: See the whole experience, including the feelings.
idea: A journey map follows one person through a task, including how they feel.
notes:
A user journey map visualises the steps a person takes to reach a goal, together with what they think and feel at each step. It turns scattered research into a single story.

Typical layers: stages across the top; the actions the user takes; the touchpoints they use, such as a poster, app or email; their thoughts; an emotional curve showing highs and lows; and opportunities for design improvement.

The emotional curve is the most powerful part. The lowest point marks the biggest pain, which becomes the highest priority opportunity. Notice here that the dip happens at registration, when a long form causes frustration.

Important: this map is a hypothesis for the persona Aisha. A real journey map must be built from research evidence, using interviews, observation and surveys, as you will do in the Unit 3 assignment. Compare it with a user flow: a journey shows feelings and context; a flow shows system steps.

eyebrow: USER PAIN POINTS AND THE CURB-CUT EFFECT
title: Fix a pain point. Many people benefit.
idea: Process, functional, financial and support pain points. Fixing one often helps many people.
notes:
A pain point is a specific problem users experience when trying to reach a goal. A helpful way to sort them is into four categories: process pain points (too many steps or an unclear path), functional pain points (something is broken or slow), financial pain points (costs, fees or surprises), and support pain points (difficulty getting help). Categorising pain points helps teams see patterns and decide priorities.

The curb-cut effect is the idea that designs created for a specific group often benefit many others. Curb cuts, the ramps built into pavements, were campaigned for by disability rights activists, yet they also help people with strollers, luggage, bicycles and deliveries.

Digital equivalents: captions help deaf users but also viewers in noisy places; large tap targets help people with motor impairments and anyone using one hand; dark mode and voice input help many contexts.

Discuss: which pain point in Gather would benefit the most students if solved well?

title: Map the path: registering for an event.
idea: A user flow shows steps and decisions from start to success, here for registering.
notes:
A user flow is a diagram of the steps a user takes to complete a task, including decisions and alternative paths. It focuses on logic and screens rather than feelings, which is the difference from a journey map.

Standard flowchart conventions: rounded shapes mark where the flow starts or ends; rectangles are steps or screens; diamonds are decisions with labelled yes and no branches; arrows show direction.

Read the Gather flow aloud. A student opens the app, browses or searches, views details and the system asks: are they logged in? If not, they sign in with a campus ID and rejoin the flow. They choose a session and ticket, complete details, and the system checks seats. If seats are available they receive a confirmation and QR ticket plus a reminder; if not, they join a waitlist and are notified if a place opens.

A good flow reveals unnecessary steps and missing error paths before any screen is drawn. This flow becomes the basis for the wireframes in Unit 4.

title: Choose the method that answers your question.
idea: Attitudinal or behavioural, qualitative or quantitative: pick the method that answers your question.
notes:
Research methods differ in two key ways, often shown on a landscape of methods popularised by the Nielsen Norman Group. Attitudinal methods capture what people say; behavioural methods capture what people do. Qualitative methods explain why and how; quantitative methods measure how many and how much.

Interviews are one-to-one conversations that reveal motivations and context. Surveys collect opinions from many people cheaply. Observation and field studies watch behaviour in real settings. Usability studies ask people to complete tasks with a design to expose where it fails. Other methods include focus groups, diary studies, card sorting and analytics.

Key message: what people say and what they do often differ, so combine methods. Early in a project, use qualitative methods to explore; later, use quantitative methods to measure. Christian Kraft's User Experience Innovation and Joel Marsh's UX for Beginners both discuss user research in practical terms.

title: What people say, think, do and feel.
idea: An empathy map captures what people say, think, do and feel.
notes:
Empathy tools help you step into someone else's experience.

The empathy map, popularised by XPLANE, organises what you know about a user into four areas: what they say, think, do and feel. Gaps and contradictions between the quadrants, for example saying "I'm fine" while feeling anxious, are often where the best insights live.

Interviews are a core empathy tool. Ask open questions that invite stories, such as "Tell me about the last event you went to", rather than closed questions that invite yes or no. Follow up with "why" to dig deeper, and stay silent to give people time to think.

Observation reveals behaviour that people forget or cannot describe. Watch what they do, not only what they say. Always listen for motivations: goals, needs and context.

The map shown is a hypothesis for Aisha. In your assignment you will populate it with real research.

title: From groups of users to one clear persona.
idea: Group users by behaviour, then write one persona grounded in what you found.
notes:
User segmentation divides your audience into groups that share needs, behaviours or characteristics. Segments can be based on demographics, but in UX, behaviour and familiarity are usually more useful. For Gather we might segment by how often students attended events last semester: high, moderate and low engagement.

Always write explicit criteria before you recruit, so that each participant clearly belongs in one segment. The criteria shown are examples.

A persona is a fictional but research-based character that represents a segment. Alan Cooper popularised personas in software design. A good persona includes a name and photo, context, goals, frustrations, behaviours and a quote, so the team can make decisions by asking "what would Aisha need?"

Warning: this persona is a proto-persona based on assumptions. A real persona must be built from your own research findings, as in the Unit 3 assignment. Never invent research and present it as fact.

eyebrow: USABILITY, HEURISTIC ANALYSIS AND FIELD TESTING
title: Three ways to find usability problems.
idea: Usability testing, heuristic review and field testing each catch different problems.
notes:
These three evaluation approaches answer different questions.

Usability testing observes real users attempting realistic tasks with a design, usually in a lab or remotely. It shows where people actually struggle and yields measures such as success rate and time on task.

Heuristic evaluation is an expert inspection. Evaluators review an interface against recognised principles, most famously Jakob Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, and list problems with severity ratings. It is fast and cheap, but experts are not real users.

Field testing, or field studies, observes people using a product in their real environment, such as a student registering on a crowded bus. It captures context, interruptions and constraints that a lab cannot.

Use heuristics early to catch obvious problems, usability tests to learn how users behave, and field tests to check real-world fit. Tullis and Albert's Measuring the User Experience explains the metrics.

The ten heuristics are shown at the bottom for reference.

title: Research real users. Build a persona.
idea: Assignment 3: plan research, recruit, segment users and write a persona.
notes:
Unit 3 assignment: create a user research plan, recruit respondents, prepare questions and task scenarios, record answers, segment users into high, moderate and low engagement or familiarity groups using explicit criteria, and develop a persona from the findings.

Stress three points. First, write the segmentation criteria before recruiting and justify them; for example, number of events attended last semester or time since first using a registration app. Second, ethics: get informed consent, protect privacy and explain how data will be used. Third, evidence: every goal, frustration and quote in the persona must trace back to something a participant said or did. Do not invent quotes.

Encourage students to recruit a small but varied group and to plan at least one realistic task scenario, such as "You want to register for a workshop on Friday. Show me how you would do that."

The criteria shown on this slide are examples only. The submission format is set by the instructor.

eyebrow: UNIT 4  ·  VISUAL HIERARCHY, SCALE AND PROPORTION
title: Make the important thing look important.
idea: Scale, contrast and weight tell people what matters first.
notes:
Visual hierarchy is the arrangement of elements so that people see them in order of importance. It guides the eye and reduces effort. The main tools are scale (size), contrast (weight and colour), position, spacing and proportion.

Compare the two screens. In the before version every line has the same size, weight and colour, so the eye has nowhere to land, and the call to action is a tiny link. In the after version, the title is large, the date and place are clearly grouped, a spacious hero draws attention, and the Register button is the strongest element on the screen.

Scale signals importance. Contrast separates levels. Proportion means using consistent ratios between sizes and spaces, such as a type scale where each step is about 1.25 times the previous one, so the design feels orderly rather than random.

Try the squint test: blur your eyes. What stands out first? If it is not the most important element, adjust the hierarchy.

title: Be consistent. Then vary on purpose.
idea: Keep patterns consistent so the product feels like one thing, then vary with purpose.
notes:
Unity and variety are a pair of design principles that must be balanced.

Unity means the parts of a design belong together: they share colour, typography, spacing, shape and behaviour. Consistency reduces learning effort, because once a person understands one button they understand them all. It also builds trust and a recognisable identity. Repetition, such as identical cards in a list, creates rhythm.

Variety adds interest and signals importance. A design with only unity can feel monotonous; a design with only variety feels chaotic. The key word is meaningful: vary something to communicate, for example highlighting a featured event with an inverted colour, not just for decoration.

On the left, the four buttons look unrelated, so users must wonder whether they behave differently. On the right they form a family. On the cards, three are identical and one is different, so the difference means something. This links to Jakob's Law and consistency in Nielsen's heuristics.

title: Four decisions behind every interface.
idea: Type, colour, icons and layout are four decisions that shape every screen.
notes:
These four areas are the foundations of interface design decisions.

Typography: choose one or two typefaces and a type scale, a set of sizes related by a ratio. Body text is commonly set at 16 px or more with a line height around 1.5 and line lengths of about 45 to 75 characters. Hierarchy comes from size and weight.

Colour: define roles, not just swatches. Primary for key actions, secondary for supporting elements, neutrals for text and backgrounds, and semantic colours for success, warning and error. A simple guide is the 60-30-10 rule: mostly neutral, some secondary, a little accent. Always check contrast.

Iconography: use one consistent style, with the same stroke, corner and size. Pair icons with labels unless the meaning is universal.

Layout: use a grid and a spacing system, such as multiples of 8, so alignment and rhythm are consistent. Group related items with proximity.

This deck itself uses Inter, a restrained palette and an 8-point rhythm.

title: The brain groups what it sees.
idea: Proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, figure-ground and common region.
notes:
Gestalt psychology studies how people perceive whole patterns rather than isolated parts. Designers use these principles to make interfaces easy to scan and understand without extra explanation.

Proximity: items that are close together are seen as a group, so keep labels near their fields. Similarity: items that look alike are seen as related, which is why links share a colour. Continuity: the eye follows smooth lines and curves, which is why a partly visible carousel card invites scrolling. Closure: we complete incomplete shapes, so a loading ring or a simple logo can be minimal. Figure-ground: we separate a focal object from its background, as with a dialog over a dimmed page. Common region: items inside the same boundary are seen as a group, which is why cards work.

Yablonski's Laws of UX covers several of these as named laws. Ask students to find one example of each in a familiar app.

title: Evaluate early, again, and after launch.
idea: Early on sketches, in the middle on prototypes, late on the live product.
notes:
Evaluation checks whether a design works. Different methods suit different stages, and the sooner you evaluate, the cheaper fixes are.

Early, with sketches and concepts: heuristic evaluation, where experts review against principles; cognitive walkthrough, where evaluators step through tasks as a new user would; and concept interviews. Middle, with prototypes: usability testing, first-click tests that measure whether people start in the right place, and card sorting or tree testing for information architecture. Late, with a live product: A/B testing to compare versions, analytics to see behaviour at scale, surveys such as the System Usability Scale, and field studies.

Tullis and Albert's Measuring the User Experience groups metrics into performance, self-reported, behavioural and physiological, and issue-based metrics. Choose methods based on your question, your stage and your resources, and combine qualitative insight with quantitative evidence.

title: Reading a familiar interface: a music app home.
idea: A teaching read of a familiar music app home screen. Observations to test, not facts.
notes:
This case study analyses a pattern familiar from music streaming apps such as Spotify. The screen is an original schematic redrawn for teaching, not official artwork, and the analysis is our interpretation, not proven fact.

Use a four-step lens: observe what is on the screen, interpret why it may work using a principle, question what could go wrong, and propose an improvement to test.

For example, bottom tab navigation keeps main destinations within easy thumb reach, which relates to Fitts's Law, and mirrors the placement in many apps, which relates to Jakob's Law. Shortcut tiles may reduce effort for returning users. Horizontal shelves pack many choices into limited space, so we should ask whether the amount of choice becomes overwhelming, which connects to Hick's Law. A persistent mini-player keeps system status visible. Grey secondary text on a dark background must still meet contrast requirements.

Ask students to validate each question with a quick usability test rather than assuming the answer.

title: Write requirements from the user’s side.
idea: A user story, its acceptance criteria and a use case, all written from the user's side.
notes:
User stories and use cases turn research into clear requirements.

A user story is a short statement from the user's perspective: "As a [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit]." The benefit is vital because it explains why. Good stories are often checked against the INVEST criteria: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable.

Acceptance criteria define when the story is done. A common format is Given, When, Then: given a starting state, when the user acts, then a specific, testable result happens.

A use case is more detailed. It names an actor, preconditions, the main flow step by step, alternate flows for exceptions, and the postcondition. A scenario is a short narrative of a person in context, used to bring requirements to life.

For Gather, the story, criteria and use case on this slide all describe the same feature, registering for an event. Notice how the alternate flow, a full event, matches the flow chart from Unit 3.

title: Organise content so people can find it.
idea: Group, label and link content so people can find it without thinking.
notes:
Information architecture, IA, is the structural design of content: how it is grouped, labelled, ordered and linked so people can find and understand it. Garrett places information architecture on the Structure plane.

Four ideas to teach. Grouping: put related content together, ideally informed by card sorting, where users group topics themselves. Labels: use words users understand, not internal jargon. Content hierarchy: decide what is primary and what is secondary. Navigation structure: choose a pattern that fits the content, such as hierarchy for deep content, a flat tab bar for a few main areas, hub-and-spoke where users return to a home, and a sequence for step-by-step tasks like checkout.

The sitemap shows Gather's structure. The blue path is a route map: the path one user takes through the structure for one task. Compare it with a user flow, which adds decisions and system logic.

Tree testing can verify whether people can find items in a proposed structure before you design any screens.

title: Map the experience. Then wireframe it.
idea: Assignment 4: choose a method, map a flow, then wireframe at two fidelities.
notes:
Unit 4 assignment: choose a method, create a route map or user flow, then design low-fidelity and high-fidelity wireframes for the proposed experience.

Explain the sequence. The method, for example card sorting or a user flow, gives structure to the experience. The route map or flow shows how a user will move through it. Low-fidelity wireframes explore layout and content priority quickly in greys, without colour distractions. High-fidelity wireframes add typography, colour, imagery and realistic content, applying the hierarchy, Gestalt and consistency principles from this unit.

Students should be able to trace each wireframe back to a step in their flow, and explain their visual hierarchy choices. They should also reference the user research and persona from Unit 3.

Remind students to design for both mobile and web in Unit 5. The submission format is set by the instructor.

title: Define the problem. Make a testable bet.
idea: Name the problem, then state a hypothesis you can actually test.
notes:
Before testing anything, you need to know what you are testing and what would count as success.

A problem statement describes who has a need and why, based on research insight. A common structure is: [User] needs [need] because [insight]. It is not a solution in disguise. A related tool is the How Might We question, which turns the problem into an invitation to ideate, such as "How might we help students register without missing deadlines?"

A hypothesis is a testable prediction: We believe that [change] for [users] will [outcome]. We will know we are right when [measure]. It must be specific and falsifiable. If the test result could not prove you wrong, it is not a hypothesis.

The weak statement "Make registration better" has no user, no change and no measure. The strong version can be tested in a usability session. The criterion of four of five participants is an example of a planned success criterion you set in advance, not a finding.

Ask students to rewrite a vague goal as a hypothesis.

title: Draw the boundary. Stay honest.
idea: Map direct, indirect and alternative competitors, and spot four deceptive patterns.
notes:
Two ideas about boundaries.

First, competitive scope. You cannot analyse everything, so decide where to draw the line and say why. Direct competitors solve the same problem for the same users; indirect competitors solve it differently, such as a campus web page; alternatives are non-digital substitutes like posters and word of mouth. Document your scope and reasons so others can challenge it.

Second, ethics. Deceptive patterns, also called dark patterns, are interface tricks that push people into choices they did not intend. Harry Brignull coined the term dark patterns in 2010 and maintains the site deceptive.design. Examples shown: confirmshaming (guilt-trip wording on the decline button), pre-ticked opt-ins, fake urgency, and roach motels where joining is easy but leaving is hard.

Designers are responsible for the effects of their work. Ethical UX respects user autonomy, is honest, and makes consequences clear. Ask: would this still work if the user fully understood what we are doing?

title: Fidelity: how finished should it look?
idea: Low fidelity is fast and cheap to change. High fidelity looks real and tests detail.
notes:
Fidelity describes how closely a wireframe resembles the final product. Choosing the right level saves time and gets better feedback.

Low-fidelity wireframes use greys, boxes, placeholder images and basic text. Their purpose is to explore structure, layout and content priority quickly. Because they look unfinished, people give feedback on the idea rather than on colours, and they are cheap to change. Use them early, in team discussions and sketching sessions.

High-fidelity wireframes add real typography, colour, imagery, spacing and realistic content. They show the near-final look and feel, so they suit stakeholder reviews, usability testing that needs realism, and hand-off to developers. They take longer to create and change.

Both phones show the same Gather event screen. Notice the layout is identical; only the level of detail changes. A good workflow moves from low to high fidelity as decisions firm up. Joel Marsh's UX for Beginners explains wireframing for newcomers.

title: Four screens carry the whole registration.
idea: Four mobile screens carry Gather registration: home, detail, form, success.
notes:
This is the mobile wireframe set for Gather, drawn at low fidelity. It follows the user flow from Unit 3: Home, Event details, Register, and Confirmation. Each screen has one clear job.

Home helps students browse and filter events. Details presents key facts and one primary action. Register is a short form with visible labels and the information pre-filled. Confirmation shows the QR ticket and next steps.

Mobile wireframing principles: design for one hand, with key actions in easy thumb reach near the bottom; keep one primary action per screen; prioritise content because space is limited; use real content, not lorem ipsum, so you can judge hierarchy and length; make it obvious how to go back.

Use standard platform patterns such as a bottom navigation bar, which helps Jakob's Law. Check the screens against your flow and run the checklist on the right before moving to prototyping.

title: The same experience, rebuilt for a wide screen.
idea: The same task redesigned for a wide screen with a different layout.
notes:
Now the equivalent desktop experience for the event details screen. The content and flow are the same as on mobile, but the layout uses horizontal space: a large hero and description on the left, and a sticky registration panel on the right so the primary action stays visible while scrolling.

Responsive considerations. Design mobile first: start with the smallest screen, decide what is essential, then add space and secondary content as the screen grows. Use breakpoints where the layout genuinely breaks, not simply at device names. On desktop expect mouse and keyboard, so provide hover and visible focus states. On tablet and phone expect touch, so targets must be larger. Content priority must stay the same across sizes: the registration action is never hidden.

The three diagrams show how the grid reflows: three columns, two columns, then one. Also test text size and zoom to 200 percent.

title: A prototype tests behaviour, not pictures.
idea: Prototypes test behaviour: can a person finish the task?
notes:
A prototype is an interactive simulation of a product, built to learn something before investing in development. Wireframes show what screens contain; prototypes show how they behave.

Navigation: hotspots, the blue dashed areas on the screens, link one screen to another so people can tap through a flow. Transitions: motion between screens, such as a slide or fade, explains change and keeps orientation. Keep them short; interface animations are commonly a few hundred milliseconds. Interaction states: every control should be designed for default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading, error and success, because real users encounter all of them.

Fidelity has two dimensions: visual detail and interaction depth. Paper prototypes are great for quick checks; clickable wireframes test flow; high-fidelity prototypes test feel; coded prototypes test technical feasibility. Match fidelity to your question. Tools such as Figma support all of these.

In Unit 5 you will build an interactive prototype of Gather and test it.

title: Watch real people try real tasks.
idea: Give people real tasks, watch quietly, and record what happens.
notes:
Usability testing puts a prototype or product in front of representative users and observes them completing realistic tasks. The five steps are: recruit participants who match your target users; brief them, explaining that you are testing the design and not them; give task scenarios; observe and note what happens without helping; and measure.

Scenario and task: a scenario gives context without revealing how to do the task, for example "You are a first-year student and a friend mentions Design Week. Find the keynote and register." Avoid leading words such as "tap the Register button".

Measures from Tullis and Albert's Measuring the User Experience: task success, time on task and errors; self-reported measures such as the Single Ease Question, SEQ, after each task and the System Usability Scale, SUS, at the end; plus observations and quotes. Small rounds of around five participants often reveal many major problems; repeat after each redesign.

The results grid is an empty template. We deliberately show no invented results. Fill it with your own data.

title: Turn feedback into the next, better version.
idea: Critique with I like, I wish, What if. Prioritise by impact and effort, then iterate.
notes:
Feedback is only valuable when it changes the design. The workflow is: observe, prioritise, redesign, retest.

Analysing feedback: group observations into themes, note how many participants hit each problem, and separate what people did from what they said. Prioritising: weigh the impact on users against the effort to fix. The matrix on the left is a simple tool: quick wins with high impact and low effort come first; major projects need planning; fill-ins can wait; and low-impact, high-effort items should be reconsidered. Usability problems are often also rated by severity, considering frequency, impact and persistence.

The findings in the matrix are hypothetical, to demonstrate the method. Your own matrix must come from your test data.

Design critique is a structured conversation. A simple protocol is I like, I wish, What if: strengths first, then constructive improvements, then new ideas. Critique the design against goals, not the designer. Then redesign, retest, and repeat.

title: Prototype it. Test it. Improve it with evidence.
idea: Assignment 5, the capstone: wireframes, prototype, test, document and revise.
notes:
Unit 5 assignment, the capstone: create low- and high-fidelity wireframes, build an interactive prototype, conduct usability testing, document findings, and revise the design based on evidence.

This is where the course outcome is demonstrated: students should be able to create mobile and web wireframes and working prototypes. Expect the work to cover both mobile and web, and to show a clear traceable chain from hypothesis, to test, to finding, to design change.

Grading focus (set by the instructor): quality of the wireframes and prototype; a rigorous test plan with realistic tasks; honest documentation, including problems that were found; and revisions that are justified by evidence. Remind students not to invent data. A modest test with real participants is better than a polished fake one.

Suggest a before and after comparison of at least one screen so the improvement is visible.

title: From idea to experience.
idea: From idea to experience: the whole process in one loop.
notes:
Close the course by walking around the loop once. Research: understand people through interviews, observation and surveys. Define: write the problem and a testable hypothesis. Ideate: diverge, then converge on solutions. Structure: information architecture, user flows and route maps. Wireframe: low then high fidelity, for mobile and web. Prototype: make it interactive. Test: put it in front of users and measure. Iterate: use the evidence to improve, and start again.

Key takeaways. One: UX is the whole experience and UI is one layer of it. Two: start with people, using research, empathy and inclusive design. Three: structure comes before surface. Four: prototype and test early; evidence beats opinion. Five: design is never finished, only iterated.

Reinforce the final outcome: students should now be able to create mobile and web wireframes and working prototypes, and to justify their decisions with evidence.

Course references: Yablonski, Laws of UX; Garrett, The Elements of User Experience; Marsh, UX for Beginners; Kraft, User Experience Innovation; Tullis and Albert, Measuring the User Experience. Thank students and invite questions.
